subject: Geography
sub_topic: Ocean salinity — factors affecting (evaporation, precipitation, river inflow, ice melting)

concepts.name: Average Ocean Salinity: Composition and Benchmark Values
key_dimensions: Average salinity of 35 ppt (parts per thousand) as baseline and how it is measured
Dominant salts: NaCl (~77.7%) vs. other salts (MgCl2, MgSO4) — proportional composition trap
Difference between salinity in open ocean vs. coastal/enclosed seas
Why salinity is expressed in ppt or PSU (Practical Salinity Units) and not percentage

concepts.name: Evaporation as a Salinity-Increasing Factor: Latitudinal Patterns
key_dimensions: Mechanism: evaporation removes freshwater, leaving salts behind — concentrating effect
High evaporation zones (20°–30° N/S subtropical belts) and their high-salinity correlation
Why equatorial regions have HIGH evaporation but LOWER salinity than subtropics — a classic UPSC trap
Seasonal variation in evaporation rates and consequent salinity fluctuations

concepts.name: Precipitation as a Salinity-Reducing Factor: Equatorial Anomaly
key_dimensions: Mechanism: rainwater dilutes surface salinity directly
Equatorial low-pressure belt: high precipitation overrides high evaporation, resulting in lower salinity than subtropical highs
ITCZ migration and its seasonal impact on salinity in Indian Ocean and Bay of Bengal
Comparison: Pacific equatorial salinity vs. Atlantic equatorial salinity due to differential precipitation

concepts.name: River Inflow and Its Diluting Effect on Coastal/Enclosed Water Bodies
key_dimensions: Freshwater input from rivers lowers salinity near river mouths and deltas (e.g., Amazon, Ganges-Brahmaputra)
Seasonal variation: monsoon discharge vs. dry season — Bay of Bengal salinity fluctuation
Why Bay of Bengal has lower salinity than Arabian Sea despite both being in Indian Ocean
Estuarine salinity gradient: halocline formation at river-sea interface

concepts.name: Ice Melting and Freezing: Polar Salinity Dynamics
key_dimensions: Ice melting adds freshwater → reduces salinity (Arctic summer, Antarctic meltwater)
Sea ice FORMATION expels salt (brine rejection) → increases local salinity and triggers thermohaline circulation
Asymmetry: Arctic vs. Antarctic salinity patterns due to landmass configuration and ice sheet dynamics
Climate change implication: accelerated glacial melt → freshening of polar oceans → disruption of AMOC

concepts.name: Latitudinal Variation of Ocean Salinity: The Double-Maxima Pattern
key_dimensions: Salinity double maxima at ~25°N and ~25°S (subtropical highs) and minimum near equator and poles
Explaining the M-shaped or W-shaped salinity-latitude graph — a frequent diagram-based question
Role of atmospheric pressure belts (Horse latitudes vs. Doldrums) in creating this pattern
Comparison between Northern and Southern Hemisphere salinity curves and reasons for asymmetry

concepts.name: Horizontal Distribution of Salinity: Ocean-Wise Comparison
key_dimensions: Atlantic Ocean has highest average salinity (~37 ppt) among major oceans — reasons (narrow width, high evaporation, fewer rivers)
Pacific Ocean has lower salinity than Atlantic despite being largest — reason: more precipitation, larger freshwater input
Indian Ocean salinity: Arabian Sea (~37 ppt) vs. Bay of Bengal (~32 ppt) contrast and causative factors
Arctic Ocean: lowest salinity among oceans due to ice melt and river inflow (Ob, Yenisei, Lena)

concepts.name: Vertical Distribution of Salinity: Halocline and Depth Profiles
key_dimensions: Surface layer: variable salinity controlled by evaporation, precipitation, river input
Halocline: zone of rapid salinity change with depth — analogous to thermocline for temperature
Deep ocean: relatively uniform salinity (~34.5–35 ppt) — reasons and significance
Absence of halocline in polar regions and its implication for vertical mixing and thermohaline circulation

concepts.name: Enclosed and Semi-Enclosed Seas: Extreme Salinity Anomalies
key_dimensions: High salinity anomalies: Red Sea (~41 ppt), Persian Gulf (~38–40 ppt) — reasons: high evaporation, low precipitation, no river inflow, restricted exchange
Low salinity anomalies: Baltic Sea (~10 ppt) — reasons: abundant river input, low evaporation, limited ocean exchange
Dead Sea (not ocean but often compared): ~330 ppt — endorheic basin dynamics
Mediterranean Sea paradox: higher salinity than Atlantic but outflow goes INTO Atlantic — Gibraltar exchange dynamics

concepts.name: Wind and Ocean Currents as Indirect Factors Affecting Salinity Distribution
key_dimensions: Trade winds drive high-salinity subtropical surface water toward equator — horizontal mixing mechanism
Warm currents carry high-salinity water to higher latitudes (e.g., Gulf Stream raises North Atlantic salinity)
Cold currents (e.g., Labrador, Benguela) bring lower-salinity water to subtropical coasts
Upwelling zones: bring deep, slightly saltier water to surface — salinity increase near upwelling coasts

concepts.name: Thermohaline Circulation (THC): Salinity as a Density Driver
key_dimensions: Salinity increases density → drives deep-water formation in polar regions (NADW, AABW)
Role of brine rejection during sea ice formation in triggering thermohaline circulation
Difference between temperature-driven and salinity-driven density changes — halosteric vs. thermosteric effects
Disruption of THC by freshwater influx (glacial melt) — 'ocean conveyor belt' slowdown scenario

concepts.name: Arabian Sea vs. Bay of Bengal Salinity Contrast: A Classic UPSC Comparison
key_dimensions: Arabian Sea (~36–37 ppt) vs. Bay of Bengal (~30–32 ppt) — quantitative values
Factors: Bay of Bengal receives Ganga, Brahmaputra, Irrawaddy; Arabian Sea receives no major rivers
Bay of Bengal gets heavy monsoon rainfall; Arabian Sea is more arid on surrounding landmass
Consequences: Bay of Bengal more stratified → less upwelling → lower productivity than Arabian Sea

concepts.name: Salinity and Marine Life: Ecological Implications
key_dimensions: Optimal salinity range for marine organisms — stenohaline vs. euryhaline species
Coral reefs and their sensitivity to salinity changes (alongside temperature) — bleaching context
Mangroves thriving in brackish water — salinity tolerance as an adaptation
Impact of reduced salinity (due to glacial melt or heavy precipitation) on marine biodiversity and fisheries

concepts.name: Salinity and Freezing Point of Seawater: Physical Properties
key_dimensions: Higher salinity → lower freezing point (seawater freezes at ~−1.8°C vs. freshwater at 0°C)
Implication: polar seas do not freeze uniformly — Arctic vs. Antarctic sea ice seasonality
Density maximum concept: freshwater is densest at 4°C but saline water behaves differently
Practical relevance: navigation in polar routes, ice-free ports, Arctic shipping lane viability

concepts.name: Salinity Measurement: Tools, Units, and Modern Monitoring
key_dimensions: Historical: titration (Knudsen method) vs. modern: electrical conductivity (CTD sensors)
Remote sensing: NASA's Aquarius satellite and SMOS for surface salinity mapping — first such global dataset
PSU (Practical Salinity Unit) vs. ppt — conceptual difference and why PSU is dimensionless
Argo floats: autonomous profiling of salinity and temperature at depth — significance for climate monitoring

concepts.name: Seasonal Variation in Ocean Salinity: Monsoon and Polar Examples
key_dimensions: Bay of Bengal: dramatic seasonal salinity drop during southwest monsoon (June–September) due to rainfall and river discharge
Arctic Ocean: summer melt season reduces salinity; winter freezing raises it via brine rejection
Mediterranean: summer high salinity (high evaporation, low rainfall); winter relative dilution
Implication for seasonal halocline development and stratification affecting nutrient upwelling

concepts.name: Freshwater Budget of Oceans: Evaporation-Precipitation Balance
key_dimensions: Atlantic: E > P (net evaporator) → exports water vapor to Pacific → higher Atlantic salinity
Pacific: P > E (net receiver) → lower salinity than Atlantic — the 'salinity contrast paradox'
Global freshwater cycle: rivers return ~37,000 km³/year to oceans — balancing the evaporative loss
Climate change impact: intensified hydrological cycle → 'salty gets saltier, fresh gets fresher' pattern observed by IPCC

concepts.name: Impact of Climate Change on Ocean Salinity Patterns
key_dimensions: Accelerated glacial and ice sheet melting → freshening of Arctic and North Atlantic → potential AMOC weakening
Intensification of global water cycle: wet regions get wetter (lower salinity), dry regions get drier (higher salinity)
Sea level rise and coastal salinity intrusion into estuaries, groundwater, and agricultural land
IPCC AR6 findings on observed salinity changes as a 'rain gauge' for tracking hydrological cycle intensification

concepts.name: Salinity Gradients and Osmotic Energy (Salinity Power): Emerging Application
key_dimensions: Osmotic pressure difference at river-sea interface can be harnessed for electricity (pressure-retarded osmosis)
Norway's prototype osmotic power plant at Tofte — concept and limitations
Relevance to India: estuaries of Ganga, Krishna, Godavari as potential sites
Blue energy as a renewable source — UPSC current affairs angle linking geography to energy policy
